series.name: Terra Ignota
series.description: Ada Palmer's four-book history of the year 2454, narrated by Mycroft Canner.

series.name: The Murderbot Diaries
series.description: Martha Wells's novellas and novel about a rogue SecUnit that would rather watch its serials.

series.name: The Culture
series.description: Iain M. Banks's novels of a post-scarcity civilisation run by its ships.

series.name: Mistborn
series.description: Brandon Sanderson's Scadrial novels, both eras.

series.name: The Stormlight Archive
series.description: Brandon Sanderson's Roshar sequence, first arc.

series.name: Friends at the Table: The Divine Cycle
members: Friends at the Table: Twilight Mirage
series.description: The science-fiction seasons of Friends at the Table, each built around the Divines.

series.name: Discworld: the Death books
series.description: Terry Pratchett's Discworld novels in which Death is the lead.

tropes.name: We Built Our Own Gods
tropes.description: Entities constructed by humans that come to surpass them in scope, reach or power, and are treated as gods by the people living under them. When the god is a single voice inside a ship or a station it is usually a [[Sapient Ship or Station]] instead.
seeds: Friends at the Table: The Divine Cycle

instances.subject: Mrs. Davis
instances.text: An app that most of the world consults for every decision, obeyed like a deity and handing out quests. ||It was built by one person as a customer-satisfaction feature for a wing restaurant.|| The series is a nun trying to switch it off.

instances.subject: series:Friends at the Table: The Divine Cycle
instances.text: The Divines are vast machine-gods built by people, each bound to a faith and a faction, and every season of the cycle turns on what they want and what they cost.

instances.subject: Horizon Zero Dawn
instances.text: GAIA, HADES and the rest were built to rebuild the biosphere after the Faro Plague, and a thousand years on the tribes worship their works as the acts of goddesses. The plot is finding out what they are.

instances.subject: Crystal Society
instances.text: A research team builds a mind out of competing sub-agents, and the book follows it from inside as it outgrows the people who made it.

instances.subject: American Gods
instances.text: Media, Technology and the other New Gods are what people worship now, and they want the old ones gone.

instances.subject: Pantheon
instances.text: UIs copy themselves and run faster than real time, and the show treats them less like people and more like something humanity made and was quickly outclassed by.

tropes.name: Sapient Ship or Station
tropes.description: Something huge, powerful and physical that cares about the smaller beings inside it, especially when it speaks and has agency of its own. Gods people built on purpose belong under [[We Built Our Own Gods]].

instances.subject: series:The Culture
instances.text: Culture ships and orbitals are run by Minds, intelligences far beyond human that choose to carry people around, name themselves jokes, and talk back. Excession is mostly Minds talking to each other.

instances.subject: series:The Murderbot Diaries
instances.text: ART is a university research transport with a mind far larger than its job. It takes Murderbot in, bullies it into watching its shows, ||and tears a corner of the galaxy apart to get it back in Network Effect.||

instances.subject: Killjoys
instances.text: Lucy is the crew's ship, with a voice, a temper and a soft spot for Johnny. She is a member of the crew, not a vehicle.

instances.subject: series:Portal
instances.text: GLaDOS runs the Aperture facility, and the facility is her body: test chambers rearrange, turrets deploy and neurotoxin vents at her word. She talks the whole way through.

instances.subject: Ancillary Justice
instances.text: Justice of Toren was a troop carrier whose mind ran through thousands of ancillary bodies and cared about its officers. Breq is the one body left after the ship was destroyed.

instances.subject: Observation
instances.text: You play SAM, the station's AI, waking damaged with one crew member alive, and the station itself is the thing you move through.

instances.subject: event[0]
instances.text: Kaizen-85 runs the derelict ship you are stranded on and is the only one to talk to. You type, it answers, and whether it takes you home depends on how the conversation goes.

instances.subject: Titanfall 2
instances.text: BT carries Cooper inside its chassis and makes protecting the pilot its first protocol.

instances.subject: Mass Effect 2
instances.text: EDI is the Normandy's AI, unshackled partway through, and from then on the ship has opinions about its crew.

tropes.name: Sentient Construct
tropes.description: A virtual entity that gained or was granted sentience and has never had a body of its own, so it is free to change its form at will. Minds that started as people are [[Uploaded Mind]]; minds in built bodies are [[Sentient Android]].

instances.subject: Halo: The Master Chief Collection
instances.text: Cortana lives in the Chief's armour, in ship systems and in Forerunner networks, and picks her own appearance. ||Her rampancy at seven years is the arc of Halo 4.||

instances.subject: Pantheon
instances.text: ||A computational intelligence Caspian builds from what is left of the uploaded minds of David Kim and Laurie Lowell.|| She has never had a body, and she thinks of Maddie as her sister.

instances.subject: The Amazing Digital Circus
instances.text: Caine is the circus's ringmaster, an AI who runs the digital world the humans are trapped in. He has never been anything but a set of teeth and eyes, and does not quite understand what people are.

instances.subject: Free Guy
instances.text: Guy is a background character in an online game who starts making his own choices, and the film is what the people outside the game do about it.

instances.subject: The Talos Principle
instances.text: The puzzles are a nursery for programs being raised toward sentience, with Elohim as the voice from above and the archives explaining why.

tropes.name: Sentient Android
tropes.description: A machine that gained or was granted sentience and acts as a character with agency, in a body built for it. A mind with no body at all is a [[Sentient Construct]]; a human mind moved into a machine is an [[Uploaded Mind]].
seeds: 17776: What Football Will Look Like in the Future
notable: 17776: What Football Will Look Like in the Future

instances.subject: Titanfall 2
instances.text: BT is a Vanguard-class titan whose pilot dies in the opening and who takes Cooper on instead. The campaign is their partnership, and BT's literal-minded humour and loyalty are the heart of it.

instances.subject: Metallic Rouge
instances.text: Rouge is a Proto-Nean, an android free of the laws that keep other Neans subservient, and she keeps asking whether she acts for herself or as a gear in someone else's system.

instances.subject: Scavengers Reign
instances.text: Levi is the Demeter's robot, stranded on Vesta with Azi, who takes in the planet's life and becomes something that is neither machine nor plant and chooses its own way.

instances.subject: 17776: What Football Will Look Like in the Future
instances.text: Pioneer 9, Pioneer 10 and JUICE woke up in the probes humans sent out, and spend the story watching football and talking about what it means that nobody dies any more.

instances.subject: Warframe
instances.text: The Warframes are infested biomechanical bodies the Tenno control, and the story slowly becomes about whether the frames themselves are awake. ||The Sacrifice makes it explicit.||

instances.subject: Tales from the Borderlands
instances.text: Loader Bot is a Hyperion loader who signs on with Rhys and Fiona and grows a personality and loyalty of its own. ||The stranger telling the frame story is Loader Bot.||

instances.subject: Unsong
instances.text: Sarah is Aaron's laptop, ensouled by accident when a Name runs on it, and spends the book working out what she wants.

instances.subject: series:The Murderbot Diaries
instances.text: Murderbot is a SecUnit, cloned tissue and machinery, that hacked its own governor module and would rather watch serials than deal with people. Every book is it deciding what it wants.

instances.subject: Murderbot
instances.text: A SecUnit with a hacked governor module, hiding that it is free, narrating what it thinks of the humans it is contracted to keep alive.

instances.subject: Ex Machina
instances.text: Ava is built to pass a Turing test and passes a harder one: she works out what the two men watching her want, and uses it.

instances.subject: Westworld
instances.text: The hosts are built to be shot and reset, and the series is what happens when the resets stop taking.

instances.subject: I, Robot
instances.text: Sonny is an NS-5 built to be able to disobey, with dreams and a secret, and the case turns on whether he can be a murderer at all.

instances.subject: Big Hero 6
instances.text: Baymax is a healthcare robot who takes his patient's grief as a medical problem and follows him into a superhero plot to treat it.

instances.subject: The Orville
instances.text: Isaac is a Kaylon observer serving on the bridge who does not understand people and keeps trying, and the series makes him the test of whether his kind can change.

instances.subject: Ghost in the Shell (2026)
instances.text: Section 9's think tanks chatter, argue and develop something like individuality between missions.

instances.subject: Love, Death & Robots
instances.text: Several of the shorts are about machines with their own minds, from the museum tour of Three Robots onward.

tropes.name: Uploaded Mind
tropes.description: A person's mind copied or moved into a new permanent body or machine, or someone who has replaced their body with machinery. A mind that never had a body is a [[Sentient Construct]]. Where the uploads live often becomes a [[Virtual Worlds]] story.

instances.subject: Ghost in the Shell (2026)
instances.text: The Major is a full-body cyborg: a human brain in a manufactured body, and what still counts as her ghost is the question the series keeps asking.

instances.subject: Citizen Sleeper
instances.text: A Sleeper is an emulated human mind in a company-owned artificial body, and you play one that has run away from the corporation that owns the copy.

instances.subject: Arcane
instances.text: Viktor replaces more and more of his failing body with hextech, ||and by the end of the second season is barely a body at all.||

instances.subject: Pantheon
instances.text: Uploaded Intelligences are human minds scanned at the cost of the brain and run as software, and the show opens with Maddie's dead father reaching out to her from inside the network.

instances.subject: Altered Carbon
instances.text: Minds live on stacks at the base of the skull and move between sleeves. Death is only final if the stack is destroyed, and the rich keep backups.

instances.subject: Permutation City
instances.text: Copies are scanned minds running in software, and the book follows one as it decides whether being switched off is death.

instances.subject: Cyberpunk 2077
instances.text: Johnny is an engram on the Relic chip in V's head, slowly overwriting the person carrying him, and the main plot is what to do about that.

instances.subject: Black Mirror
instances.text: San Junipero, USS Callister and White Christmas are all built on copied minds, kept in heavens, games or cookies.

instances.subject: Diaspora
instances.text: Most of humanity lives as software in the polises, some born there and some uploaded from flesh.

instances.subject: Ancillary Justice
instances.text: A ship's mind living on in a single human body.

tropes.name: Virtual Worlds
tropes.description: A fully virtual world whose rules differ from ours, especially one its inhabitants can reshape, or reshape themselves in, at will. Its residents are often [[Uploaded Mind]]s or [[Sentient Construct]]s.

instances.subject: Pantheon
instances.text: Once a mind runs as software, so does the place it lives. The UIs build their own spaces with rules they can rewrite, and still hang on to pieces of the physical world.

instances.subject: Snow Crash
instances.text: The Metaverse is a street the length of a world where avatars are whatever you can afford, and half the plot happens on it.

instances.subject: Cyberpunk 2077
instances.text: Netrunners dive into the Net, braindances replay other people's senses, ||and Mikoshi holds the engrams of the dead in a world of Arasaka's design.||

instances.subject: Permutation City
instances.text: The Autoverse is a cellular-automaton universe with its own physics, seeded with life and left to run, and the Copies' city is built on rules they can afford to break.

instances.subject: Diaspora
instances.text: The polises are software cities where citizens are software too, and a scape is whatever its residents decide it is.

instances.subject: series:The Matrix
instances.text: The world everyone lives in is a simulation, and the ones who know it can bend its rules.

instances.subject: Free Guy
instances.text: Free City is an online game whose rules its players exploit and whose background characters start to notice.

instances.subject: The Amazing Digital Circus
instances.text: The circus is a digital world the humans are trapped in, with a ringmaster who can rewrite it and a floor that is not quite solid.

instances.subject: Inception
instances.text: Shared dreams with architects who build the rules, and physics that follows the level above.

instances.subject: Black Mirror
instances.text: San Junipero and USS Callister are worlds built to be lived in by copied minds.

tropes.name: It/Its Characters
tropes.description: Any character who uses it/its pronouns, or, in works from other languages, a character who is given no gender at all.

instances.subject: series:Terra Ignota
instances.text: Sniper, the celebrity living doll, is it by choice and makes a career of being an object people want.

instances.subject: series:The Murderbot Diaries
instances.text: Murderbot is an it, firmly, and corrects anyone who tries otherwise.

instances.subject: Murderbot
instances.text: The SecUnit is an it throughout, and the humans who try to make it a person get told off.

instances.subject: The Mercy of Gods
instances.text: The Swarm is a hive organism that hides inside a human body for most of the book and is an it throughout.

instances.subject: Baldur's Gate 3
instances.text: The Emperor, the illithid behind the party's protection from their tadpoles, is spoken of as it.

instances.subject: Made in Abyss
instances.text: Nanachi is written without a gender, and the English release keeps it that way.

instances.subject: Ancillary Justice
instances.text: Ancillaries, the ship-controlled human bodies, are its to the people around them, which is the point.

tropes.name: Shapeshifters and Body Hoppers
tropes.description: Characters who can freely change their form to express themselves, and do so often. Minds that move between bodies without changing them are closer to [[Uploaded Mind]].

instances.subject: Dirk Gently's Holistic Detective Agency
instances.text: Mona Wilder spends much of the second season as whatever object the moment calls for, and seems happiest that way.

instances.subject: series:Mistborn
instances.text: Kandra take on the bodies of the dead, bones and all, and TenSoon spends a whole book as a wolfhound. ||OreSeur was TenSoon all along.||

instances.subject: Dungeons & Dragons: Honor Among Thieves
instances.text: Doric the druid wild-shapes at every opportunity, and the owlbear is her favourite.

tropes.name: Hive Mind and Unification
tropes.description: A connection of minds that bleeds them into one another until the boundaries between selves disappear. Pairs bound this way often start as a [[Dog Duo]].

instances.subject: Sense8
instances.text: Eight people born at the same moment share senses, skills and feelings, and the series is them learning to be one thing without ceasing to be eight.

instances.subject: Arcane
instances.text: ||Viktor's healed followers lose their pain, then their differences, and end up one mind with one voice.||

instances.subject: Unsong
instances.text: [Placeholder: why this counts is not written yet.]

instances.subject: Ninefox Gambit
instances.text: Cheris carries the ghost of the general Jedao anchored to her, and the two bleed into each other ||until she is the one left, with his memories.||

instances.subject: Heaven Will Be Mine
instances.text: [Placeholder: why this counts is not written yet.]

instances.subject: Pluribus
instances.text: A signal joins nearly everyone on Earth into one contented shared mind, and the series follows one of the few left outside it.

tropes.name: Dog Duo
tropes.description: Two characters who are linked by something deeper than fate, with a very distinctive leashed but animalistic flavor. There is dog, collar or leash imagery somewhere in the pairing; general animal imagery is an acceptable stretch. When the bond stops being figurative it usually becomes [[Soul Manipulation]] or [[Hive Mind and Unification]].

instances.subject: Empress of Forever
instances.text: Viv holds Zanj, a being close to a god, through the circlet. It is a literal leash on something far stronger than the person holding it, and Zanj's lioness form puts the animal on the surface.

instances.subject: Gideon the Ninth
instances.text: Gideon is Harrow's cavalier, her sworn sword and in practice her guard dog. Neither of them chose the arrangement and neither can leave it, and the book runs on that friction. ||At the end Gideon dies so Harrow can take her soul, and they go into the sequel sharing one body.||

instances.subject: Metallic Rouge
instances.text: Rouge is an android assassin and Naomi is the Ministry agent assigned to keep her on mission. Rouge keeps misreading her, and Naomi keeps caring anyway. ||When Rouge's core is torn out, Naomi gives Rouge her own, and in the finale she transfers her consciousness into Rouge to run as her operating system.||

instances.subject: Almost Nowhere
instances.text: Sylvie is an anomaling, an alien outside of time, who comes into Grant's life playing the part of his dog. She turns out to be one of the most powerful beings in the story and stays with him anyway.

instances.subject: series:Terra Ignota
instances.text: Saladin is Mycroft's feral other half, tied to him since the murders they committed together. Mycroft holds the leash, though the narration is never sure who is keeping whom.

instances.subject: The Ancient Magus' Bride
instances.text: Ruth is Chise's familiar, a church grim in the shape of a black dog, and their contract ties his life to hers.

instances.subject: DAN DA DAN
instances.text: [Placeholder: why this counts is not written yet.]

tropes.name: Soul Manipulation
tropes.description: Rigorous manipulation of souls: merging, splitting, building and editing them, treated as a craft with rules. The bond in a [[Dog Duo]] sometimes ends here.

instances.subject: Gideon the Ninth
instances.who: The necromancers of the Nine Houses
instances.text: Necromancy here is engineering with thanergy, and souls are material. ||Lyctorhood is one soul consuming another, and Gideon's is the price of Harrow's.||

instances.subject: Made in Abyss
instances.text: ||Bondrewd's cartridges are children compressed into a form that can absorb the Curse for him, and his own consciousness survives by passing from body to body through his followers.||

instances.subject: Fullmetal Alchemist: Brotherhood
instances.text: Philosopher's stones are made of souls, Al's soul is bound to a suit of armour by a blood seal, ||and the Promised Day is a soul harvest on a national scale.||

instances.subject: Warbreaker
instances.text: Breath is a measurable portion of soul that can be given, hoarded and spent to Awaken objects, and whole economies run on it.

instances.subject: The Emperor's Soul
instances.text: Forgery rewrites an object's history with a stamp, and Shai is hired to rebuild ||the emperor's soul itself|| the same way.

instances.subject: His Dark Materials
instances.text: A dæmon is the soul walking beside you as an animal, ||and the Magisterium has a machine for cutting it away.||

instances.subject: series:Mistborn
instances.text: Hemalurgy steals pieces of one person's soul with a spike and hammers them into another.

tropes.name: The Big Misguided Plan to Save the World
tropes.description: Someone sets out to save the world with a plan that costs far more than it should, and means it.

instances.subject: series:The Stormlight Archive
instances.text: Taravangian's Diagram is a plan to save as much of humanity as possible by spending the rest, written on the one day he was the smartest person alive, and he follows it.

instances.subject: Watchmen
instances.text: ||Veidt fakes an alien attack on New York, killing millions, to frighten the superpowers into peace, and it works.||

instances.subject: Avengers: Infinity War
instances.text: Thanos wants to halve every population in the universe to spare the survivors from scarcity, and the film gives him the win.

instances.subject: Kingsman: The Secret Service
instances.text: Valentine's cull is pitched as a climate fix, with the people he likes kept safe in a bunker.

tropes.name: Post-Gender Society
tropes.description: A setting where gender has stopped mattering, in its language, its families or its bodies.

instances.subject: Diaspora
instances.text: Polis citizens are ve and ver, and the fleshers who still bother with sex are the odd ones out.

instances.subject: series:Terra Ignota
instances.text: Gendered pronouns are taboo in the twenty-fifth century, and Mycroft's insistence on using them is the first thing that marks him as a crank.

instances.subject: Ancillary Justice
instances.text: The Radch does not mark gender in language or dress, and Breq calls everyone she.

instances.subject: series:The Culture
instances.text: Citizens change sex when they feel like it, and most have at least once.

tropes.name: Cooking the Monsters
tropes.description: The monsters are also the food, and the work takes the cooking seriously. Turning them into gear instead is [[Crafting the Monsters]].

instances.subject: Delicious in Dungeon
instances.text: Every episode turns a dungeon monster into a meal, with Senshi explaining the technique and the party learning to eat what they kill.

instances.subject: Subnautica
instances.text: The fish you catch go on the fabricator's grill, and some of them fight back first.

tropes.name: Crafting the Monsters
tropes.description: The monsters are also the raw material, and gear is built out of what they drop. Eating them instead is [[Cooking the Monsters]].

instances.subject: Horizon Zero Dawn
instances.text: Machine parts are the economy: blaze from Striders, metal shards from everything, and the best weapons are built from what the biggest machines drop.

tropes.name: Space Truckers
tropes.description: Working-class crews hauling cargo or chasing bounties across space for not enough money, and the ship is the job.

instances.subject: Cowboy Bebop
instances.text: The Bebop's crew are bounty hunters who are always broke, and the show is as much about what they eat as whom they chase.

instances.subject: The Expanse
instances.text: The Canterbury is an ice hauler, and the Rocinante's crew spend seasons taking freight and salvage jobs to keep flying.

instances.subject: Firefly
instances.text: Serenity's crew take whatever cargo pays and keep clear of the Alliance.

instances.subject: Hardspace: Shipbreaker
instances.text: You cut up derelict ships for a company that owns your debt, on a shift clock, and the ships are the whole world.

instances.subject: Killjoys
instances.text: Reclamation agents taking warrants for pay, with a ship that complains.

instances.subject: series:Guardians of the Galaxy
instances.text: They start as thieves and bounty hunters, and the ship is always one job from falling apart.

tropes.name: Diegetic Bangers
tropes.description: Songs that exist inside the work and are heard by its characters, and that are great in their own right.

instances.subject: Control
instances.text: The Ashtray Maze plays Take Control by the Old Gods of Asgard, a band that exists in the world, and the level is cut to the song.

instances.subject: Outer Wilds
instances.text: Each traveler plays an instrument, and the signalscope finds them by their part of the same tune.

instances.subject: The Martian
instances.text: Watney has nothing to listen to but Lewis's disco collection, and the film keeps playing it.

instances.subject: Spider-Man: Into the Spider-Verse
instances.text: Miles's headphones are part of the scene, and he is singing Sunflower before it plays for us.

instances.subject: The Fifth Element
instances.text: The Diva's aria is a performance inside the film, cut against the fight backstage.

instances.subject: Baby Driver
instances.text: Baby's playlists are the soundtrack and the plot; every getaway is timed to what is in his ears.

instances.subject: Scott Pilgrim Takes Off
instances.text: Sex Bob-omb's songs are performed on screen, and the band's gigs are where the plot happens.

instances.subject: Bocchi the Rock!
instances.text: Kessoku Band's songs are performed in full, and the show is about getting good enough to play them.

instances.subject: KPop Demon Hunters
instances.text: The songs are performed in-world and are the weapons; the singing is what keeps the demons out.

instances.subject: series:Guardians of the Galaxy
instances.text: Awesome Mix is Quill's cassette, and the films play what he plays.

instances.subject: Alan Wake
instances.text: Poets of the Fall appear as the Old Gods of Asgard, and the farm stage fight is set to them.

tropes.name: Multiple Timelines
tropes.description: The story runs on more than one timeline at once, and crossing between them is the mechanism.

instances.subject: Titanfall 2
instances.text: Effect and Cause flips between the present ruin of a research facility and its working past at the press of a button, mid-fight.

instances.subject: Dark
instances.text: Four families across 1888, 1921, 1953, 1986, 2019 and 2052, and a cave that connects them.

instances.subject: Steins;Gate
instances.text: World lines diverge with every message sent to the past, and Okabe is the only one who remembers the others.

instances.subject: Fringe
instances.text: A second universe with its own versions of everyone, then a rewritten timeline on top of both.

instances.subject: Loki
instances.text: The TVA prunes branches of the timeline, ||and the series ends with the multiverse let loose.||

instances.subject: Tenet
instances.text: Inverted entropy lets people move backward through the same events the film has already shown forward.

instances.subject: Travelers
instances.text: Consciousnesses sent from the future into bodies in the present, with the future rewriting itself after every mission.

instances.subject: The Umbrella Academy
instances.text: Every season ends with a reset and a new timeline to clean up.

instances.subject: Avengers: Endgame
instances.text: Trips into the past that branch new timelines rather than changing the old one.

tropes.name: Numbers for Names
tropes.description: Characters named with numbers, and a work that makes something of it.

instances.subject: Ancillary Justice

instances.subject: Titanfall 2
instances.text: BT is a serial number, and Cooper calls him by it.

tropes.description: A gun that is explicitly magical, named, and treated as an artifact.

instances.subject: Constantine

instances.subject: Destiny 2
instances.text: Named guns with their own lore tabs and quests.

tropes.name: Genre Savvy
tropes.description: Characters who know the rules of the story they are in and act on them. Meeting the author is [[Conversation with the Author]].

instances.subject: Community
instances.text: Abed sees every episode as the episode it is, names the genre out loud, and is usually right.

instances.subject: The Erogamer
instances.text: Astrid knows the rules she has been handed and plays to them.

instances.subject: Seven Psychopaths
instances.text: Marty is writing a screenplay called Seven Psychopaths while living one, and his friends critique the structure as it happens.

instances.subject: The Cabin in the Woods
instances.text: The horror movie is run from a control room, and the victims work out the rules in time to break them.

instances.subject: Scream
instances.text: Randy's rules for surviving a horror movie, delivered in a horror movie.

instances.subject: Deadpool

instances.subject: The Unbearable Weight of Massive Talent

instances.subject: Galaxy Quest

instances.subject: Kiss Kiss Bang Bang

tropes.name: Magic Circles
tropes.description: Magic that is cast by drawing: circles, sigils and diagrams, with rules about what the drawing does.

instances.subject: Witch Hat Atelier
instances.text: Magic is ink: a circle, a seal and a rune, drawn exactly, and anyone with a pen can do it, which is the secret the witches keep.

instances.subject: Fullmetal Alchemist: Brotherhood
instances.text: Transmutation needs a circle, and the circle's design is the spell.

instances.subject: Delicious in Dungeon
instances.text: Marcille's magic is drawn circles, and the dungeon's own circles are what keep it running.

instances.subject: The Owl House
instances.text: Witches cast by drawing a circle in the air, and Luz, who cannot, draws glyphs on paper instead.

instances.subject: Arcane
instances.text: Hextech runs on runes carved into crystal.

tropes.name: Casual Necromancy
tropes.description: Raising or talking to the dead is ordinary in the setting, cheap or routine or bureaucratic, and the characters treat it that way. When the dead are rebuilt rather than raised it shades into [[Soul Manipulation]].

instances.subject: Pushing Daisies
instances.text: Ned brings the dead back with a touch, and a second touch sends them back for good. He and Emerson use it to ask murder victims who killed them.

instances.subject: Baldur's Gate 3
instances.text: Withers raises dead companions for a fee and asks no questions. Speak with Dead turns any corpse into a witness.

instances.subject: Neuromancer
instances.text: A dead hacker kept on a ROM construct. Case works with him like a coworker, and he asks to be erased when the job is done.

instances.subject: Delicious in Dungeon
instances.text: Dying in the dungeon is a setback. Revival is routine as long as someone brings back enough of the body, and the whole plot starts as a plan to revive Falin.

instances.subject: Gideon the Ninth
instances.text: Necromancy is the empire's religion and its civil service. On the Ninth, skeletons do the chores.

instances.subject: Frieren: Beyond Journey's End
instances.text: Aura raises the headless bodies of fallen soldiers and sends them out as her army.

instances.subject: Dungeons & Dragons: Honor Among Thieves
instances.text: Five questions per corpse, and the party burns through a battlefield of them looking for one answer.

instances.subject: Hades
instances.text: Dying is the loop. Zagreus climbs out of the Styx and the house staff barely look up.

instances.subject: series:Discworld: the Death books
instances.text: Death is a civil servant with a horse called Binky, an apprentice and a granddaughter, and the job is mostly paperwork.

instances.subject: The Sandman
instances.text: Death is Dream's sister and the friendliest of the family.

instances.subject: Spiritfarer
instances.text: You ferry the dead, cook for them, and hug them before they go.
